how_it_wins:
Start with the card everyone misreads. Yawgmoth is a draw engine that happens to own a kill. "Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature: Put a -1/-1 counter on up to one target creature and draw a card" costs no mana at all — the price is a life and a body, so it runs at instant speed, on any turn, under any tax anybody at the table can name. He hits the battlefield on turn four in 7,249 of 10,000 goldfish runs, mean 4.283, and he is down by turn six in 91.7% of them.

Here is the part that should change how you sit down. The engine is not tutor-dependent. By turn 10 you have renewable fodder in 73.6% of games unassisted and 90.3% with a tutor allowed to fill the gap, a free sacrifice outlet in 73.8% / 90.0%, an ignition source in 73.0% / 90.2%, and a drain in 66.9% / 87.7%. Read every one of those as a pair — the first number excludes tutors, rituals and cost reducers entirely. Three quarters of your games hand you the engine off the top of your library. Pace for that game, because it is the median one.

What the five tutors buy is the finish, and you own four of them. Blowfly Infestation plus Nest of Scarabs goes 2.6% to 32.1% by turn 10. The Mikaeus package goes 1.7% to 26.2%. Exquisite Blood plus South Wind Avatar goes 2.9% to 32.5%. Warren Soultrader plus Gravecrawler plus any drain goes 1.1% to 20.0%. Those four are independent and nothing stops two of them showing up in the same game, so the honest quantity is their union — and the union is not reported. It is strictly greater than 32.5%. The sheet's composite line spans only two of the four; it is not your kill rate, so do not carry it to a table as one.

Now the number that decides your turns. A fully assembled engine does not have one drain rate — it has two, and they are nearly a factor of two apart. Yawgmoth plus Nest of Scarabs plus a death-metering drain is seven drains, 7 per opponent, 28 across the pod, and seven is a proven ceiling. Put Mirkwood Bats in that same slot on that same board and it is thirteen, 13 per opponent, 52 across the pod. Count the bodies before you start, not during. And remember what Grave Pact does to the same chain: every creature of yours that dies makes each other player sacrifice one, so the drain is the visible clock and the edicts are the half that actually wins fair games.

combo_lines.001: Savour the intervening "if" — it is the whole case. "Whenever a creature dies, if it had a -1/-1 counter on it, put a -1/-1 counter on target creature." That condition is checked twice, once when the trigger would go on the stack and again on resolution, and the Insect Blowfly Infestation just marked is still wearing its counter when it dies. So the loop is genuinely unbounded. The holding nobody expects: on a thin board it is also nearly drainless. State-based actions kill the counter-bearing token before the Nest trigger resolves, Blowfly is mandatory and needs a target, and the only creature left is your drain — which dies on iteration one for a total of 3 per opponent. Carry this to the table: the loop needs the drainer plus two other creatures on the battlefield when it starts. With that third body, 38 completed iterations take four opponents from 40 to 0.
combo_lines.002: The clause that bounds everything is four words: "up to one target creature." Yawgmoth is a 2/4 who could happily eat four counters, except protection from Humans makes him untargetable by his own ability — and he is a Human Cleric. Every counter has to land somewhere else, and once the opponent's body is gone the only legal targets are your own tokens. The plain holding: bodies bound this engine, and the board's number is seven. Five completed activations, seven of your creatures dead, seven Bastion of Remembrance triggers, 28 life off the pod, and your own total goes up rather than down. Spend the proliferate and it is eight drains and 32 — a property of the line, not of the board, and the two figures are never blended.
combo_lines.003: The elegant point here is that Zulaport Cutthroat is a creature, which makes it both a legal target and a legal sacrifice — and you are never forced to spend it. The sacrifice is chosen when the cost is paid, and "up to one target creature" lets you take zero targets, so neither half of the ability can reach your drain against your will. You keep it through activations one to four and then feed it deliberately, where its own leaves-the-battlefield trigger looks back in time and banks the seventh drain. The holding: five activations plus one proliferate, seven creature deaths, 7 life from each opponent, 28 across the table. The cap is structural — a drain that meters deaths is itself a body that must eventually die.
combo_lines.004: Two words decide this one: "target player." Blood Artist reads "target player loses 1 life and you gain 1 life," and at a four-player table that is one seat per trigger where Zulaport Cutthroat and Bastion of Remembrance charge all of them. The board's number is eight — eight creature deaths, eight triggers, eight life, and an exhaustive search of the line space finds nothing better. This is refuted as a kill, and not narrowly: 8 against the 28 the same shape of board produces with an each-opponent drain, a 3.5x penalty for one word of templating. Play Blood Artist as reach and insurance. Never as the finish.
combo_lines.005: The crux is CR 119.9, and it is the sharpest edge in the deck. An Insect you sacrifice dies at toughness 1, so South Wind Avatar gains you 1 and its second ability drains the table. An Insect killed by its own -1/-1 counter dies at toughness 0 — you gain 0, and gaining 0 is not a life gain event, so nothing drains. Eight death triggers, seven nonzero gains, seven drains for 28 opposing life. The Avatar's 4 toughness is worth exactly +4 activations, which is most of why the chain reaches eight at all. Spellbook tags this pairing "Near-infinite"; on this board that tag is wrong, and the ceiling is proved by case exhaustion over how the Avatar leaves.
combo_lines.006: This is a two-rule case and picking the right rule matters. CR 122.6 covers an object given counters as it enters the battlefield, and 122.6a assigns those counters to the object's controller when the effect names no player — which is you. That is not 608.2c, the rule the other stacks lean on, because 608.2c names the controller of the spell or ability instead. The holding: a creature that ENTERS with a -1/-1 counter does trigger Nest of Scarabs, and Persist is a Nest trigger as well as a reanimation. Fume Spitter comes back as a 0/0 and dies immediately; the trigger had already triggered and does not care. One divergence worth knowing: a creature entering under an opponent's control with a counter has that counter put on by them, so "whenever you put" would not fire.
combo_lines.007: Read the trigger condition slowly, because the whole result hides in it: "Whenever you create or sacrifice a token." Nothing on this line is sacrificed — the Insects go to the graveyard as state-based actions for having 0 toughness, which is the game moving a permanent, not you sacrificing one. So Mirkwood Bats collects the creation half only, twice, for 2 life from each opponent. Worse than a death-metering drain by one. And then the finding that should reorganise how you sequence: Bats is a 2/3, so when Blowfly is forced to target it, it survives at 1/2. Nothing dies. Blowfly never triggers again. An unbounded engine simply switches off, and the property responsible is the one that looks like an upgrade — extra toughness.
combo_lines.008: The legalese is the timing of a cost, and it pays. Activating Yawgmoth puts the ability on the stack first; the cost — 1 life and "Sacrifice another creature" — is paid last, as the final step of activation. So sacrificing an Insect triggers Mirkwood Bats while Yawgmoth's ability is already the topmost object, and the Bats trigger goes on ABOVE it and resolves first. The Nest token does not arrive until two resolutions later, which is the second trigger. One activation, two drains. The holding: thirteen Bats triggers, 13 per opponent, 52 life off a four-player table, against the like-for-like 7 and 28 a death-metering drain produces on the identical board. Thirteen is a ceiling, proved five separate ways, and the final check solved the line varying only Bats' toughness: 8, 10, 13 and 15 triggers at zero, one, two and three counter slots. Same card as stack 007, same 2/3 body, opposite verdict — surviving the forced counter is fatal to a loop that needs something to die and free money on a line that sacrifices deliberately.

card_roles.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: The engine, and he draws before he kills: "Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature: Put a -1/-1 counter on up to one target creature and draw a card" costs no mana, so no tax and no Winter Orb effect ever touches it. Protection from Humans cuts both ways — it blanks a slice of the format's removal and it makes him untargetable by his own ability, which is exactly what bounds every verified engine line here.
card_roles.Nest of Scarabs: The hub. "Whenever you put one or more -1/-1 counters on a creature, create that many 1/1 black Insect creature tokens" replaces the body an activation spends — one only, and only after the death, so the loop is body-neutral only while the counter lands on something that lives. Worth knowing: the retrieval graph has no entry for it at all, so the deck's most important card is invisible to the synergy shortlist.
card_roles.Mirkwood Bats: The best drain you can have and the worst, depending entirely on the line. On the Yawgmoth engine it collects both halves of "whenever you create or sacrifice a token" for a verified 13 triggers and 52 pod life; on the Blowfly loop it collects two and halts the engine outright, because its 2/3 body survives the forced counter and nothing dies. Know which line you are on before you cast it.
card_roles.Ayara, First of Locthwain: The other creation-side payoff, and the answer to a structural problem: Bastion, Zulaport, Blood Artist and South Wind Avatar all meter deaths, and Nest's Insects are black, so Ayara gets paid when they arrive. Her second ability, "{T}, Sacrifice another black creature: Draw a card," is a free outlet that draws — a second Yawgmoth for one body a turn. Her exact rate against the verified 13 and 7 is not yet measured; play her as a payoff, not as a promise.
card_roles.Bastion of Remembrance: A death-metering drain that cannot be eaten by your own engine, because an enchantment is never a legal target or a legal sacrifice. Verified at seven drains and 28 pod life on a full board, eight and 32 if you spend the proliferate. Its enters-the-battlefield Human Soldier is a real body — count it.
card_roles.Zulaport Cutthroat: Each opponent, every death, and you gain the life back — the cleanest drain in the deck at two mana. Verified at seven drains and 28 across the pod, and the cap is structural: it is itself a body the engine must eventually consume. You are never forced to spend it early, so don't.
card_roles.Blood Artist: Reach, and only reach. "Target player loses 1 life" is one seat per trigger, which the checker measured at 8 total life against 28 for an each-opponent drain — a 3.5x penalty at a four-player table. Deploy it happily; just never plan the kill around it.
card_roles.South Wind Avatar: A 4-toughness sink that is worth exactly +4 activations to the engine, plus a drain that reads "whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life." The trap is precise: a token killed by its own counter dies at toughness 0, you gain 0, and gaining 0 is not a life gain event — so sacrifice your Insects rather than counter-killing them when the Avatar is out. It is also half of the only bracket-3 line in the 99.
card_roles.Exquisite Blood: "Whenever an opponent loses life, you gain that much life" — pointed straight at South Wind Avatar, whose drain feeds it and which it feeds back. That is the highest-bracket line the deck contains and the goldfish already models it at 2.9% unassisted and 32.5% tutor-assisted by turn 10. The loop itself is unresolved, so hold it as a plan, not a proof.
card_roles.Blowfly Infestation: A genuinely unbounded engine with Nest of Scarabs and a firm entry requirement: your drain plus two other creatures on the battlefield when it starts, or Blowfly's mandatory trigger is forced onto the drain and the whole thing pays 3 per opponent and stops. Meet the requirement and 38 iterations kill a four-player table.
card_roles.Grave Pact: The asymmetry converter and the deck's only edict. "Whenever a creature you control dies, each other player sacrifices a creature of their choice" turns a chain the drain ledger scores at seven life into seven edicts per seat — a one-sided board wipe you were paying for anyway. Against creature pods this is the card that wins, not the drain.
card_roles.Gravecrawler: Fodder at {B}, recast from the graveyard forever as long as you control a Zombie — and you build that condition for free, since Warren Soultrader, Gray Merchant of Asphodel, Mikaeus and Stitcher's Supplier are all Zombies, Grave Titan makes them, and Nim Deathmantle turns its wearer into one. Every recast is a body for an outlet and, with a creation-side payoff out, a drain trigger.
card_roles.Reassembling Skeleton: The unconditional floor of the fodder class: "{1}{B}: Return this card from your graveyard to the battlefield tapped," forever, with nothing to satisfy on the battlefield. That is the fodder that survives a wrath, and it is why an empty board is still an engine turn if you have two mana.
card_roles.Warren Soultrader: Three jobs in one slot — a free repeatable outlet, a Treasure per sacrifice, and a Zombie body that switches Gravecrawler on. Its cost is 1 life, the same currency Yawgmoth spends, so with any drain that gains you a life the loop reads neutral rather than negative.
card_roles.Pitiless Plunderer: Death converted straight into castable mana: every other creature of yours that dies makes a Treasure. It is one of five cards the sheet counts as engine mana, a class you have by turn 10 in 60.6% of games unassisted and 85.0% assisted — the second-thinnest resource in the deck, so this body is worth protecting.
card_roles.Gray Merchant of Asphodel: A one-shot drain sized by devotion in a deck carrying 75 black pips across 54 cards, which is about as much devotion as mono-black gets. It is also a Zombie for Gravecrawler and a reanimation target for Persist, Victimize, Animate Dead and Nim Deathmantle — so it drains more than once if you play it that way.
card_roles.Mikaeus, the Unhallowed: Seven of the deck's eleven two-card infinites name him, and none of them is verified. Undying returns a creature only "if it had no +1/+1 counters on it," so the loops need something to strip the counter each cycle — and Yawgmoth's -1/-1 counter does exactly that. Treat him as an enormous ceiling with an open question underneath, and read the finding in the combo section before you announce a line.
card_roles.Carnifex Demon: The self-shrinking body the Mikaeus package is built around: "{B}, Remove a -1/-1 counter from this creature: Put a -1/-1 counter on each other creature" is repeatable ignition, mass removal and a pile of Insects in one activation. Six mana is a real cost; get it back by pointing it at a board, not at your own tokens.
card_roles.Massacre Girl, Known Killer: Every creature you control gains wither, which means your combat damage arrives as -1/-1 counters and every one of them triggers Nest of Scarabs. The draw clause only reads opponents' creatures, so this is a removal engine that pays you for pointing it outward.
card_roles.Skinrender: Three -1/-1 counters on entry — that is a kill on most bodies and three Insects at once, from a single event. One of the most efficient ignition sources in the deck and a Zombie besides.
card_roles.Soul Snuffers: "Put a -1/-1 counter on each creature" is a one-sided sweeper in a deck that wants counters, because every counter on your own side becomes an Insect. Sequence it before you commit tokens you care about, not after.
card_roles.Fume Spitter: One mana, one counter, one Insect, and it sacrifices itself to do it — the cheapest ignition in the deck and a body for a death trigger in the same card. It is the piece that starts the Blowfly loop.
card_roles.Black Sun's Zenith: A sweeper that is also ignition, which is the only reason a deck like this can run four wipes without wiping itself: counters you place on creatures already on the battlefield trigger Nest of Scarabs. The token count from one multi-creature X is not settled, so size X for the board you want gone and treat the Insects as upside.
card_roles.Toxic Deluge: The cleanest answer in mono-black to a board you cannot race, and with a drain out every body it kills pays you. Be exact about the interaction: -X/-X is not counters, so Nest of Scarabs does not trigger off it.
card_roles.Blasting Station: A free outlet that also converts each body into a point of damage to any target, and it untaps whenever a creature enters — which the Insects do. That is reach that ignores lifegain and blockers entirely.
card_roles.Carrion Feeder: A one-mana free outlet that grows, and a named half of one of the Mikaeus two-card lines. It cannot block, so it is a sacrifice engine wearing a creature's body, not a defender.
card_roles.Viscera Seer: One mana, free outlet, and the scry smooths every engine turn you take. Small card, enormous number of activations.
card_roles.Woe Strider: A free outlet that arrives with its own fodder — the 0/1 Goat — and escapes from the graveyard for {3}{B}{B} when the board gets swept. Two bodies and a recursion plan in one three-drop.
card_roles.Yahenni, Undying Partisan: A free outlet whose activation grants itself indestructible until end of turn, which answers every wrath that says destroy and every removal spell that does. Feed it in response, then keep your engine.
card_roles.Ashnod's Altar: The free outlet that pays: two colourless per sacrifice, no tap, no summoning sickness. It produces nothing coloured under the mana audit's unconditional rule, so read it as speed and as a sacrifice engine rather than as fixing.
card_roles.Phyrexian Altar: A free outlet that adds one mana of any colour per body — the version that actually recasts Gravecrawler out of the graveyard. It anchors more contained infinite lines than any other artifact in the 99.
card_roles.Phyrexian Tower: A land that is a free sacrifice outlet and makes {B}{B} doing it. In a deck where a spare creature is a resource, this is one of the best untapped lands you can draw.
card_roles.Nim Deathmantle: It returns nontoken creatures from your graveyard for {4} and makes whatever it lands on a black Zombie — which switches Gravecrawler on and, with a creation-side payoff out, means a black creature entering every cycle. Its two-card line with Ashnod's Altar is contained but unresolved; play it first for the recursion.
card_roles.Skullclamp: The second draw engine, and the one that works when the commander is answered. "+1/-1" kills a 1/1 on equip and draws two, and this deck makes 1/1 Insects, Faeries and Pests all game. One precision: that is a static modification, not a counter, so equipping never triggers Nest of Scarabs.
card_roles.Plumb the Forbidden: Your answer to the wrath, and it turns the wrath into cards instead of a rebuild: sacrifice N creatures in response and you copy the spell N times for N+1 cards and N+1 life. The role taxonomy has no pattern for it at all, which is a gap in the taxonomy and not in the card.
card_roles.Bitterblossom: A Faerie every upkeep for 1 life, forever, without spending a card — the best two-drop in the deck and the one that rebuilds through a sweeper on its own. Cast it on turn two every time you can.
card_roles.Sedgemoor Witch: A Pest for every instant and sorcery you cast, ward against removal, and menace on a 3/2. Every one of those tokens is a Yawgmoth activation.
card_roles.Black Market Connections: Three modes each turn and you choose one or more: a Treasure, a card, or a 3/2 body. In a deck that treats life as fuel this is fodder, draw and engine mana on one enchantment — and you set the price each upkeep.
card_roles.Grave Titan: Six power across three bodies on arrival, all of them Zombies, which means fodder plus Gravecrawler's condition in a single card. Deathtouch makes it a real blocker while the engine sets up.
card_roles.Butcher Ghoul: Undying fodder: it dies, it comes back, it dies again — two activations from one card, and the +1/+1 counter it returns with cancels neatly against a -1/-1 counter later.
card_roles.Geralf's Messenger: Undying plus a two-life ETB drain, so it charges an opponent twice for one card. The triple-black cost is real; the 75-pip black load is what makes it castable.
card_roles.Stitcher's Supplier: Mills three when it enters and three more when it dies, filling the graveyard for Persist, Victimize, Animate Dead and Agadeem's Awakening. A one-mana Zombie that is fodder and setup at once.
card_roles.Necroskitter: The punish card: any creature of an opponent's with a -1/-1 counter on it that dies comes back under your control. Every ignition source in the deck is quietly a theft spell while this is out.
card_roles.Sinister Gnarlbark: A card and a -1/-1 counter every end step, which in this deck is a card, an Insect and a drain trigger every end step. Blight targets a creature you control, so keep a spare token around to receive it.
card_roles.Necropotence: The deck's biggest draw engine and its bluntest: pay life, exile cards, get them at your next end step. You are already treating life as a resource everywhere else, so price it the same way here.
card_roles.Deadly Dispute: Two cards and a Treasure for two mana, with a sacrifice as the cost — which in this deck is not a cost. Instant speed makes it a removal-response as well as a draw spell.
card_roles.Castle Locthwain: An untapped black source most games and a repeatable draw for {1}{B}{B} when the board stalls. The life cost scales with your hand, so use it when you are empty, which is exactly when you want it.
card_roles.Demonic Tutor: Two mana, any card, no strings — the single most flexible card in the 99 and one of four Game Changers driving the bracket floor. Point it at the missing half of a kill, or at a rebuild when Nest of Scarabs eats removal.
card_roles.Vampiric Tutor: Instant speed, any card, on top of your library for two life. It costs you a draw step, so cast it on someone else's end step with the mana to use what you find.
card_roles.Beseech the Mirror: A tutor that can cast what it finds: bargain it by sacrificing an artifact, enchantment or token — all of which this deck makes for free — and anything with mana value 4 or less comes down without paying for it. That reaches your commander.
card_roles.Diabolic Intent: Two mana and a body for any card in the library, and the body is not a cost here — it is a death trigger. The best rate on tutoring the deck has when the board is wide.
card_roles.Insatiable Avarice: Spree lets it be a tutor for {2}, three cards for {B}{B}, or both in one cast. Flexible enough to be the setup spell early and the refuel late.
card_roles.Persist: Two mana to return a nonlegendary creature from the graveyard with a -1/-1 counter — and that counter triggers Nest of Scarabs, verified. So a reanimation is also an Insect and, with a creation payoff out, a drain.
card_roles.Victimize: One body in, two bodies out, from the graveyard, at sorcery speed. The sacrifice is a death trigger and the two returns are ETB triggers; this is the biggest single swing the recursion suite has.
card_roles.Animate Dead: Two mana to reanimate anything in any graveyard, including the best creature an opponent has already lost. The -1/-0 is nothing to a deck that wants bodies, not damage.
card_roles.Phyrexian Reclamation: A one-mana enchantment that rebuys a creature every turn for {1}{B} and two life. It is the deck's most reliable long-game engine against removal — but note it returns creature cards only, so it cannot rebuy your enchantments.
card_roles.Agadeem's Awakening // Agadeem, the Unde: A land when you need a land and a mass reanimation when you need a board — the modal card that is never dead. Pay the 3 life to have it enter untapped when the turn matters.
card_roles.Takenuma, Abandoned Mire: A black source that channels away to mill three and return a creature, cheaper for each legendary creature you control. Free value from a land slot you were playing anyway.
card_roles.Malakir Rebirth // Malakir Mire: A land or a one-mana protection spell that returns your creature to the battlefield when it dies — which also resets it and re-triggers its ETB. Hold it against targeted removal on the commander.
card_roles.Supernatural Stamina: One mana to save a creature and re-buy its enters-the-battlefield trigger, at instant speed. The taxonomy has no role pattern for it; the function is protection and a free reanimation in the same card.
card_roles.Lightning Greaves: Haste and shroud for zero equip, which gets the commander activating the turn he lands and puts him out of range of targeted removal. Mind the shroud — you cannot target him with your own tricks while it is on.
card_roles.Deadly Rollick: Free removal while you control your commander, which is most turns. Exile answers indestructible, regeneration and recursion in one word — hold it for the piece you truly cannot beat.
card_roles.Snuff Out: Four life instead of four mana while you control a Swamp, and you control 22 of them. That is instant-speed removal on a turn you tapped out to deploy the engine.
card_roles.Fatal Push: One mana for anything at mana value 2, or 4 with revolt — and revolt is on constantly here, because you sacrifice a permanent nearly every turn. The most efficient answer in the deck.
card_roles.Cabal Pit: A black source with a threshold sacrifice that gives a creature -2/-2 until end of turn. Late, on a full graveyard, it is a free removal spell out of a land slot.
card_roles.Ifnir Deadlands: A Desert that sacrifices for two -1/-1 counters on an opponent's creature — removal and two Insects from your mana base. It taps for {C} freely and for {B} at 1 life.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Turn-one Sol Ring puts the commander on the battlefield on turn two, which the sim does in 707 of 10,000 games. It makes no coloured mana, so it buys speed rather than fixing.
card_roles.Ancient Tomb: Two mana from a land for 2 life — the fastest acceleration in the deck and one of the four Game Changers on the bracket sheet. Colourless, so pair it with a black source rather than leaning on it.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Two mana for a rock that taps for black every turn after. Unglamorous, and it is the difference between the four-drop landing on turn three and on turn four.
card_roles.Dark Ritual: One black into three black, which is the whole turn-two commander plan in one card. Fast mana is the thinnest class on the sheet at 43.5% unassisted and 78.2% assisted by turn 10 — treat a Ritual in the opener as a real reason to keep.
card_roles.Command Tower: An untapped black source with no drawback whatsoever. In a mono-colour deck it is simply a Swamp that dodges a couple of narrow effects.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: Untapped and it makes black as long as any opponent's land could produce it — in a five-colour format that is nearly always. A free untapped dual in practice.
card_roles.City of Brass: Untapped, any colour, one damage when it taps. You are spending life on Yawgmoth, Necropotence and Ancient Tomb already; this is the same currency at a smaller denomination.
card_roles.Gemstone Mine: Three untapped activations of any colour and then it is gone. Games where you need it that long are games you were already winning.
card_roles.Survivors' Encampment: Taps for {C} on its own, or for any colour by tapping a creature you control — and you have spare bodies constantly. Free fixing from a board state you build anyway.
card_roles.Archway Commons: Enters tapped and asks for {1} to stick around, which is a real turn-one cost. It is here as fixing insurance in a deck that has almost none to fix.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: Enters tapped and scries when its mana casts a Cleric — your commander's type. A small tax for a small edge.
card_roles.Bojuka Bog: Enters tapped and exiles a graveyard on arrival, which in a format full of reanimation is a free answer stapled to a land. Hold it for the turn the graveyard deck is about to go off.
card_roles.Swamp: Twenty-two of them, the untapped backbone of a 36-land mana base, and the reason Snuff Out costs four life instead of four mana. In mono-black the basic is the best land in the deck.

mulligan:
The keep test is not "do I have the kill." It is: can this hand make bodies, and can it kill one of them for free? Every line in the deck routes through those two classes, and they are the two the sim finds earliest — mean turn 2.796 for renewable fodder and 2.803 for a free outlet.

You get to be picky, and you almost never have to be. The goldfish keeps its first seven 82.3% of the time at a mean of 0.209 mulligans, and its kept hands cluster hard: 3,586 with three lands, 3,422 with two, 2,226 with four. Two to five lands is your band. Below two you are hoping; above five you are drawing air, because 48 of the 64 spells cost three or less and mean available mana on turn four is 3.910.

Keep on sight: two to four lands plus something that renews a body. Bitterblossom on turn two is the best keep in the deck — a Faerie every upkeep for 1 life, no card spent, and it rebuilds through a sweeper by itself. Reassembling Skeleton and Gravecrawler are the same promise from the graveyard. Nest of Scarabs, Grave Titan, Sedgemoor Witch and Black Market Connections round out the class, and you have one of them by turn 10 in 73.6% of games unassisted, 90.3% with a tutor.

Also keep any hand with Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb or Dark Ritual and a black source. Fast mana is the thinnest thing on the sheet — 43.5% unassisted, 78.2% assisted — so a hand that already holds it is ahead of a curve most of your games never get. That is the hand that casts Yawgmoth on turn two.

Ship the inverse hand without a second thought. Four lands and three payoffs with no fodder and no outlet is a mulligan, however good the cards read: strategy:mulligans.engine-hands is blunt that payoffs without the enabler are blanks until the engine exists, while enablers at least dig toward the payoff. Ship a hand whose only sacrifice outlet is the commander you cannot cast until turn four. Ship five and six lands. And use the free first mulligan ruthlessly — 100-card singleton means you are mulliganing to enabler classes, not to named cards, and this deck built the redundancy for it.
upgrades:
Rank a slot by what it moves, and on this deck three numbers do the moving. Start with the widest one: a creation-side payoff is worth 13 drains and 52 pod life where a death-metering payoff is worth 7 and 28 on the identical board. That is verified, it is an 86% gap, and only two cards in the 99 collect on the creation side. Anything that pays when a token arrives — rather than when one dies — is buying the biggest measured margin the deck has.

The second number is fast mana, which sits at 43.5% unassisted and 78.2% assisted by turn 10 and is the thinnest class on the sheet by a distance. Three cards carry it. The commander costs {2}{B}{B} and lands on turn two in 707 of 10,000 games; every additional turn-one accelerant moves that histogram directly. Engine mana is the same argument one notch up: 60.6% and 85.0%, five cards, and it is what converts a wide board into a castable turn rather than a parked one.

The third is not a percentage, it is a shape. Nest of Scarabs is a singleton hub, it is an enchantment, and nothing in the 99 rebuys an enchantment — Phyrexian Reclamation, Persist, Victimize, Animate Dead and Agadeem's Awakening all read creature card. So a slot that closes on an axis independent of the Nest is worth more than its raw power suggests, and that is why the deck runs four named kills rather than one.

Watch what will not move, because it sets the ceiling on the conversation. The bracket floor is 4, driven by four Game Changers and eleven two-card infinites, and seven of those eleven name one card. A slot that extends an engine does not escalate the deck; a slot that adds a twelfth two-card infinite does not either, because the floor is already there. What actually raises the deck's power is verification, not addition — the same checker that measured the 13 has also refuted three lines the combo database called kills.
mana_base:
Mono-colour makes half the audit trivial and then hides the interesting question in the other half. Black is 100% of the pip load and 100% of the sources, so pip share and source share cannot disagree — there is no colour to be short of. The load itself is real: 75.0 black pips across 54 cards, up to triple-black in a single cost, and the first pip is demanded on turn one.

So the only question left is how many, and the yardstick answers it with a caveat. Thirty-six land copies across 15 entries, 22 of them Swamp, and 35 of those 36 make black — Ancient Tomb is the one that does not. The audit wants 36 sources for a 90% on-curve rate and the note is blunt about what that means in a 36-land deck: the target is a yardstick, not a possibility. Lands alone land you at 89.5%. That half-point shortfall is arithmetic, not a build error.

Ten nonland producers close it and then some. Four rocks, four rituals and two dorks lift the count to 43 sources and on-curve black to 96.0%. Read what each class actually buys. The rituals are turn-two commander mana. The dorks — Pitiless Plunderer and Warren Soultrader — are engine mana, which is a different resource: they turn a creature dying into castable black, and the sheet has that class at 60.6% unassisted and 85.0% assisted by turn 10. And mind which producers score zero under the unconditional-mana rule: Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb and Ashnod's Altar make nothing coloured, so they buy speed, never fixing. Restricted mana anywhere in the 99: none.

Four lands enter tapped — Archway Commons, Bojuka Bog, Castle Locthwain and Path of Ancestry — which is about as low a tap rate as a mana base gets, and it matters here because the commander's ability is free and instant-speed. An untapped land is an activation you can hold up.

The curve is where the 36th land earns its keep. Land-drop hit rate is 92.3% on turn three, 80.7% on turn four and 40.4% by turn ten, and mean available mana runs 3.910 on turn four to 7.103 on turn ten. Against 48 of 64 spells at mana value three or less, that is a mana base built to deploy early and then convert the flood into Reassembling Skeleton activations rather than into dead cards.
threat_assessment:
You are on the table's radar at turn four, and you should be glad about it — that is how early this engine comes online. The goldfish puts Yawgmoth on the battlefield on turn four in 7,249 of 10,000 games, mean cast turn 4.283, down by turn six in 91.7% of them. Nothing else you do is that reliable. Your best card and your first tell arrive together, so plan the whole game around that one fact.

Know exactly what three opponents read off you. The bracket report puts you at floor 4 on four Game Changers — Ancient Tomb, Demonic Tutor, Necropotence, Vampiric Tutor — eleven two-card infinites, and 42 combo lines fully contained in the 99. Add five tutors and, from across the table, you look like a combo deck wearing a sacrifice costume.

That perception is a resource, not a problem. strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection tells you the shape of it: "combo decks look non-threatening while advancing in secret, which is exactly why experienced tables hit the quiet ramp player." Read in reverse, that sentence is a description of your seat. Your quiet turns will be discounted by anyone who tracks draw engines, so spend the discount deliberately rather than hoping for it.

Now hold the number that keeps everything manageable. A fully assembled drain engine — Yawgmoth, Nest of Scarabs, a death-metering drain — produces seven drains. Stack 002 proves it with Bastion of Remembrance, stack 003 proves it with Zulaport Cutthroat, both checker-pass, both landing on seven per opponent and 28 across a four-opponent pod. The table goes from 40 to 33.

So a scary board is a clock, and the table will price it as a kill. That is my read of this deck's central political problem, and it is a sequencing problem — which is the good kind, because you solve those for free.

Two board states genuinely make you the archenemy, and both reads are correct. Mirkwood Bats on the Yawgmoth engine is thirteen triggers, 13 per opponent, 52 across the pod, 160 opposing life down to 108 (stack 008, verified five ways). Blowfly Infestation beside Nest of Scarabs with a death-metering drain and two spare bodies is the real thing — stack 001 puts four opponents from 40 to 0 in 38 completed iterations. Present either only on a turn you can act.

Grave Pact changes the room faster than any drain, and this is the political read I most want you to carry. "Whenever a creature you control dies, each other player sacrifices a creature of their choice." Stack 002's verified board kills seven of your creatures in one engine turn — seven edicts pointed at every other seat.

That extrapolation is mine, not a checked line: the seven deaths are verified, Grave Pact reads off exactly that event, and no stack has run the pair. Price it anyway. A drain takes life quietly and privately; an edict takes a creature from three players in front of everyone, every turn, forever.

So build your read hierarchy before you sit down. Bitterblossom, Reassembling Skeleton, Gravecrawler, Stitcher's Supplier and Sedgemoor Witch are furniture — they read as a fair sacrifice deck and eat almost no removal. Nest of Scarabs, Grave Pact, Mirkwood Bats, Mikaeus and Exquisite Blood are the cards that change the room.

Mikaeus deserves his own paragraph, because he is your biggest tell. He is the shared half of seven of the eleven two-card infinites on the bracket report — Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Woe Strider, Yahenni, Blasting Station. The table's correct answer to this deck is to exile him on sight. Do not teach them that.

Do not lean on him harder than the evidence does, either. Undying returns the body with a +1/+1 counter on it, which almost certainly means the loop has to route through a Yawgmoth -1/-1 to clear that counter — a three-card line, not a two-card one. None of the seven is verified; each needs a stack scenario. Treat Mikaeus as a superb value engine you would like to untap with, and let the table's fear of him do the rest.

Exquisite Blood is the opposite kind of card: it does nothing visible and it is the one nobody sees coming. With South Wind Avatar it is the highest-bracket line the report names — a candidate, not a fact, and it needs a stack scenario before you call it a kill. Deploy the Avatar first, because a 3/4 deathtouch body reads as fair. The Blood goes down on the turn it converts.

That is the general rule: lead fodder, hold the hub. Cast Nest of Scarabs on the turn it pays, not the turn you can first afford it. strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window is blunt about why — "sequence the scariest piece last so the deflection budget lasts until the turn you take it" — and with a three-card assembly, the last piece is the one everybody would have answered.

Tutors are information, so spend them at the right speed. Vampiric Tutor is an instant: fire it on the end step before your untap and the table sees a card leave your hand for a reason they cannot name until it is too late. Demonic Tutor, Diabolic Intent and Beseech the Mirror announce a plan on your main phase, so use them on turns you were already committing.

Life is your other currency, and the ledgers say the engine is not what puts you low. Stacks 002 and 003 both end with you at 42 after a full engine turn; stack 005 runs eight activations and leaves you at 39 with eight fresh cards. A drain that gains you life makes the loop life-positive.

Necropotence, Bitterblossom, Black Market Connections, City of Brass and Warren Soultrader's "Pay 1 life" are what actually drain you. Pay them freely while nobody at the table has visible reach. strategy:life-as-resource sets the discipline: know "when your life total has become real ... and switching from spending to defending one turn before it matters, not one after."

Exquisite Blood rewrites that math the moment it resolves — every point an opponent loses comes straight back to you, so a drain turn refunds the whole week's payments. With it on the battlefield, be greedier, not more careful.

Then take the window. The trigger is arithmetic done before the first activation: go when the drains your board will produce meet the lowest life total at the table. Count only board and hand. Seven with a death-metering drain, thirteen with Mirkwood Bats, and South Wind Avatar's four toughness is worth exactly four extra activations (stack 005).

One last number to keep honest, because it is the one you will be tempted to overstate. Tutor-assisted by turn ten, the four named kills sit at 32.1% (Blowfly + Nest), 26.2% (Mikaeus), 32.5% (Exquisite Blood) and 20.0% (Warren Soultrader + Gravecrawler). They overlap, so the true figure is their union — unmeasured, and strictly greater than 32.5%. The goldfish row labelled "EITHER kill" covers only two of the four; it is not your kill rate.

That modularity is the whole gift. You are never the deck that needed one card, which means you never have to defend one card. Play the engine, let the table pick a lane, and take the window when the arithmetic says yes.
matchups:
Start every game by assigning your role, then re-ask it after every board change. Against a fair pod you are the CONTROL — a commander whose ability costs no mana and converts every spare body into a card out-grinds anything fair. strategy:whos-the-beatdown gives you the operational test: "who has inevitability? — whoever loses the long game must be the beatdown." Its Commander correction is the part you will actually use: "you can be the beatdown against one opponent and the control against another in the same turn cycle; assign per-threat, not per-game."

SWEEPER CONTROL is your best matchup and you should be visibly cheerful about it. Two decks both claiming inevitability means the cheaper rebuild wins, and yours is structural rather than held: Reassembling Skeleton returns for {1}{B} forever with no board condition, Gravecrawler recasts for {B} while a Zombie is out, and Bitterblossom and Black Market Connections make a body a turn without spending a card.

So deploy fodder freely and hold the payoff. strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math says to "commit exactly as much as wins before it arrives, no further" — and here "what wins" is countable: seven drains with a death-metering drain, thirteen with Mirkwood Bats. Put the outlet and the bodies on the table; keep the drain in hand until the turn it converts.

Plumb the Forbidden is the card that flips this matchup outright. It is an instant that sacrifices any number of creatures as an additional cost and copies itself once per creature, so their wrath announcement becomes your draw step. Hold two mana whenever a control player untaps with four or more open — the standard assumption that a sweeper deck holds up its sweeper mana.

Black Sun's Zenith is your own sweeper and it profits twice. Its counters are real -1/-1 counters on each creature, so Nest of Scarabs pays you a token for every creature it touches, and Necroskitter takes back anything of theirs that dies carrying one. Toxic Deluge is the opposite and you must be precise: -X/-X is not counters, so the Nest does not trigger.

The one board state to fear is enchantment removal on Nest of Scarabs, because nothing in the 99 rebuys an enchantment. That is the case where a tutor is a rebuild rather than a finish. Spend it that way without flinching.

STAX AND TAX splits down the middle and you need to know which half you are in. "Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature" costs no mana, so a Sphere effect does not touch the engine once Yawgmoth has resolved — strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial says taxes "attack the velocity math directly, so recount your hand under the tax," and this ability is not in that hand. Deployment is your vulnerable window, not operation.

Two real exposures remain. Fast mana is three cards (43.5% unassisted, 78.2% assisted by turn ten), so a tax landing before turn four genuinely delays a commander whose mean cast turn is 4.283. And your interaction is three dedicated instants plus four sweepers, short of strategy:deckbuilding.interaction-suite's requirement that "some answers must be castable under the tax."

Name your outs out loud so you never freeze. Against Cursed Totem or a Pithing Needle on Yawgmoth, your outlets are the non-creatures: Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Blasting Station and Phyrexian Tower. Blowfly Infestation plus Nest of Scarabs is triggered rather than activated, so it runs under both — that is your kill under a lock, and stack 001 says it needs the drainer plus two spare bodies to start.

Then race the completion, not the first inconvenience. strategy:resource-hedging.playing-to-outs: identify the piece that stops YOU, not the scariest piece, and "play as if it's coming."

AGGRO makes you the pod's stabiliser and the aggressor's target at once, and this deck is unusually good at holding both jobs. Grave Pact is the card that does it: every creature you sacrifice edicts every other player, which is exactly strategy:card-advantage.virtual's Commander correction that "one tax or pillow-fort effect can blank attack plans from three players at once." You were going to run the engine anyway; against aggro it dismantles boards as a side effect.

Answer boards, not threats. Four sweepers — Toxic Deluge, Black Sun's Zenith, Carnifex Demon, Soul Snuffers — plus nine debuff effects means you have breadth here that you lack everywhere else. strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy sets the bar for your three instants at "ends the game or ends my deck's function," so do not spend Deadly Rollick on the biggest creature just because it is biggest.

Gray Merchant of Asphodel is your stabiliser and your reach in one card — devotion to black in a deck whose pip load is 75 black pips across 54 cards, drained from every opponent and gained back by you. Cast it on the turn the race is closest, not the turn it is largest.

And stop spending life one turn early. Yawgmoth's cost, Warren Soultrader's cost, Bitterblossom, Black Market Connections and City of Brass all take from the same pool the aggro deck is attacking. The drains cut back — 13 per opponent from one Mirkwood Bats assembly is 13 you did not have to race for.

COMBO is your unfavourable matchup, and against that seat you are the beatdown while remaining the control against everyone else. Your interaction on a combo turn is Deadly Rollick, Fatal Push and Snuff Out — creature removal, aimed at a kill that may not use creatures — and there are no counterspells. That is what the engine costs, and it is a fair price you pay with speed.

So hold nothing. answer-economy's countervailing clause is explicit: "against combo, or lethal already on board, the last profitable moment is now." Deadly Rollick is free while you control your commander, which is most turns from turn four.

Be the faster clock with a floor. Your four enabler classes sit at 73–74% unassisted and about 90% tutor-assisted by turn ten, and one Bats assembly removes 52 of the pod's 160 life. Pace for the engine, not for the tutored kill — the engine is the part that always shows up.

GRAVEYARD HATE earns its own paragraph, and the honest reading is that it costs you quality rather than function. Gravecrawler, Reassembling Skeleton, Persist, Victimize, Animate Dead and Phyrexian Reclamation all read from the graveyard, so a Rest in Peace effect converts renewable fodder back into one-shot fodder — precisely the axis your consistency is bought on.

But know exactly which half of your deck goes quiet, because it is not the half people assume. "Dies" means "is put into a graveyard from the battlefield" (CR 700.4, quoted in verified stacks 004 and 005), so under a graveyard replacement your death-metered payoffs stop — Zulaport Cutthroat, Bastion of Remembrance, Blood Artist, South Wind Avatar's lifegain trigger, and Grave Pact with them. That last one is the expensive part and the one nobody expects.

Your creation-side payoffs keep paying. Mirkwood Bats reads "whenever you create or sacrifice a token" and Ayara reads "enters," so both collect under hate that switches every "dies" trigger off. That is my read from oracle text, not a checked line — but it tells you which drain to tutor for when Rest in Peace is on the battlefield, and the answer is Ayara or Bats, every time.

Answer the hate on the way in. strategy:threat-assessment ranks threats partly on "interaction cost (what answering it later costs versus now)," and graveyard hate is cheap now and expensive later. Bojuka Bog is your free answer to theirs, riding on a land drop you were making anyway. It enters tapped, so drop it on a turn you were not deploying anyway — and against a graveyard deck, bank it for the turn their yard matters rather than spending it on curve.
